chapter_theme: Candakarman, sent by the king for a pair of humans to offer to the goddess, sees the brother and sister who have gone out for alms and seizes them; the brother consoles his frightened sister by teaching that the self is not harmed with the body, that deeds drive the soul through countless births, and that even gods and emperors perish, and the sister takes up the teaching and both resolve to leave the body in the Jinas' refuge.

cast.role: the elder of the twin ascetics, who comforts his sister
his young sister, who fears and then accepts
the king's officer sent to bring a pair for the sacrifice

28.reading: The two young ascetics walk the street with eyes on the ground a bow's length ahead, treading gently out of mercy for living things, and take food only from householders who receive them and offer it.
28.nuance: The bow's-length gaze is the way a Jain mendicant walks so as not to crush small lives; the poem shows the pair practising non-killing in the very street where they will be seized. Line 2, from நகை to நாணி, is damaged.
28.event: The brother and sister go through the city street on their alms round in the ascetics' manner.

29.reading: Candakarman sees the pair, whose way is to love and spare even a foe, and wonders in an unshaken mind why two so tender and fair, like Lakshmi's creeper and the god of love, have come here in youth.
29.nuance: The officer who has been sent to find a pair for sacrifice recognises the pair's gentleness and beauty at once, and the poem lets the reader feel the cost before the seizure.
29.event: Candakarman catches sight of the brother and sister and wonders at their youth and beauty.

30.reading: Having thought it over, Candakarman remembers the king's order, has his men take the two, and leads them toward the angry goddess's temple while the two wonder what has befallen them.
30.nuance: The king's order (verses 20-22) and its carrying out meet here; the poet notes the officer's doubt in verse 29 and does not let it stop him.
30.event: Candakarman seizes the two on the king's command and takes them toward the goddess's temple.

31.reading: Surrounded by harsh soldiers, the pair look like the moon joined to lightning, and the brother, seeing his sister's fear, takes her forearm and begins to speak to her.
31.nuance: The moon-and-lightning simile makes the captives bright against the dark guard; the poet names the brother by his rank as elder, not by a proper name.
31.event: Soldiers surround the pair and the brother takes his frightened sister's arm to comfort her.

32.reading: The brother tells his sister not to fear, since no destruction can come to them; any harm these men do will reach only the body, and why mourn what is not theirs, which the mind had already put aside.
32.nuance: Line 4 turns on மங்கையாம் அதனை, whose syntax is unclear; the sense here follows the plain run of the lines.
32.event: The brother tells his sister that harm to the body is no harm to the self.

claims.claim: the self cannot be destroyed, and harm done to the body is not harm to what is one's own

33.reading: The brother adds that if what is due must come, fear gains nothing and is itself pain, and that fear besides feeds deeds that like poison wear them down day by day.
33.nuance: Fear is not set aside as weakness but treated as a cause: it makes new karma, so the sibling's calm is a matter of what the next birth will be.
33.event: The brother argues that fear can neither prevent the coming harm nor do anything but add pain and karma.

claims.claim: what is due to come will come, and fearing it avails nothing
fear is itself suffering and feeds the deeds that afflict a person daily

34.reading: He says that long ago, driven by old deeds, he and his sister wandered among animals, where their own kin tormented and killed them, as they have now learned from the great sage.
34.nuance: The same pair in an earlier life were killed in animal births; the present capture is made to look like a later turn of the same wheel, not a new wrong. Line 1 has மன்னை, perhaps for அன்னை, a term of address to the sister.
34.event: The brother recalls their earlier births among animals, where their kin slew them.

claims.claim: old deeds drive the soul to wander through animal births where it is hurt and killed

35.reading: He says that, spun by deeds like a whirling wheel, they were born over and over in the four states of life, births too many to tell, and that this present moment is of the same kind.

claims.claim: deeds whirl the soul through births in the four states of existence, past counting

36.reading: He says that if in every birth they had given up the bodies they took and practised dharma, those births would not have followed them; the many who did not see what is best and did not do right have died countless deaths.
36.nuance: The syntax of lines 1-2 is a question that expects yes; the reading takes it so.

claims.claim: giving up the body and doing dharma would have stopped the birth that follows; those who do not do it die countless times

37.reading: He recounts that bodies in the hells, grown from three cubits to five hundred bows, were like those drowned in fire, and asks whether the many that came and went with them can be known.
37.nuance: The measures are the Jain cosmology's and are given as reported speech of the brother; lines 3-4 are hard.

claims.claim: bodies in hell grow in size to five hundred bows and are full of burning pain

38.reading: He says that bodies in the animal births, which grew by fine steps from the smallest fraction of a finger to five hundred, smoked in the fire of deeds, and that the pair took countless such bodies.
38.nuance: The measures of the first two lines are obscure; only the plain sense that the pair have worn countless animal bodies is firm.

claims.claim: the soul has taken countless bodies in the realm of animals under the fire of its deeds

39.reading: He says that the human bodies of earth, from one cubit up to six thousand bows, which they once took and cast off, are more than the sands of the sea.

claims.claim: the soul has taken and left more human bodies than the sea has sand

40.reading: He says that the bodies of many sizes, even those the pair took in the gods' worlds through austerity, cannot be counted, so many have perished.

claims.claim: even the heavenly bodies won by austerity are lost in their countless number

41.reading: He says that the bodies of the hell-beings, hated as the cause of pain and begging to end, and those of the gods, loved as the cause of joy and asked to stay, all perish when their day comes.

claims.claim: bodies of hell and heaven alike perish whether hated or loved

42.reading: He says that even the lords of the gods, for whom crowned heads bow before their feet and whose gold seats are held up by the heavenly, lost their own forms in countless numbers.

claims.claim: even Indra-like lords of the gods lose their forms and die

43.reading: He says that even among men, kings of kings who turn the wheel and bring all quarters under their feet, no one since their bodies arose has stood firm in the world until today.
43.nuance: Lines 3-4 turn on அக்குலத்து உடம்பு தோன்றி; the reading takes it as the line of the kings' bodies from birth to now.

claims.claim: no emperor, however great, has outlasted death

44.reading: He asks whether the loosening of a worn cloth or the leaving of one house for a richer one differs from death and birth, and bids his sister put her grief away.
44.nuance: The figure carries the argument of verses 32-43 into one daily act; its use at the moment of arrest turns a doctrine into comfort.

claims.claim: death and birth are no more than putting off a cloth or leaving a house for another

45.reading: The sister says that all her brother has taught fits those who hold the loathsome body as their own and seek only heaven's joy, and asks what the teaching is for those who have turned away even from such fruit.
45.nuance: Her question tests whether the brother's argument, which rests on the body's impermanence and heaven's loss, reaches those who want neither; the lines are loose and the reading is a best sense.
45.event: The sister puts a question to her brother about the teaching meant for those who renounce all fruit.

46.reading: The sister says that, having understood how deeds ripen into painful births and left a frightened mind without release, and the fruit of dharma the venerable sage gave, there is no fear in leaving this fearful life.
46.event: The sister says she is ready to leave the life of births.

claims.claim: deeds ripen into painful, release-less births, and the dharma the sage taught gives its own fruit

47.reading: The sister says that her brother, thinking women's minds are weak in great knowledge and firmness, spoke tenderly; but those whose minds are fixed on seeing the good dharma do not love this life.
47.nuance: The first claim is what she thinks her brother thought, not what he said; she answers it by the second, so the work can be read as turning the doubt aside without a separate reply.
47.event: The sister answers the doubt that a woman's mind is too weak for renunciation.

claims.claim: women's minds lack great knowledge and unmoving firmness
those whose minds are fixed on the vision of the good dharma do not cling to this life

48.reading: The sister says she has taken to heart what her brother taught, no longer trembles, calls him her lord, folds both hands and asks him to say plainly what she must do now.
48.event: The sister accepts her brother's teaching and asks him what to do.

49.reading: The brother says to think of the soul as different from the joined body, hold the greatness of their dharma in mind, and give up the body in the refuge of the victors; the sister gladly agrees that it is right.
49.nuance: The proposal comes as a choice to leave the body in a state of refuge, not a flight; the poem does not say how it will be done.
49.event: The brother proposes they take refuge in the Jinas and let go of the body, and the sister agrees.

claims.claim: the soul is other than the body it is joined to
taking refuge at the victors' feet and leaving the body is the right act for one who sees this

50.reading: The poet says that the two stood in the knowledge that the soul, known by its knowing and seeing, is formless, stainless and hard to grasp, is other than the body, and that tight-bound deeds are not its nature.
50.nuance: Line 3 has the odd குறுகிய தடற்றொள் வாள்போல் and the simile of a sword and its sheath is uncertain; the end of the line is read as stating the body's closeness to the soul.
50.event: The brother and sister stand firm in the knowledge of the soul's difference from the body.

claims.claim: the soul is formless and stainless, endowed with knowledge and perception, and is other than the body
karma, though bound fast, is not the soul's own nature

links.note: The king's order to Candakarman to bring a pair of humans for the goddess is carried out here as the two are seized.
links.teaches: The poem sets an officer's seeing the pair's gentleness against the order he serves, and the order wins, which shows duty to the king ruling over mercy.

links.note: The king holds that offering a pair of humans at the sword is a fitting rite; the brother holds that harm to the body is no harm to the self and so no loss.
links.teaches: The same act of killing is a gain to the king's worship and no harm to its victims in their own account, so the doomed two defuse the rite's meaning by their view of the body.

links.note: The epic says fear can neither stop the coming harm nor do anything but add pain and fresh deeds; the quatrain says the fool sighs when the fruit arrives while the wise take it as old desert.
links.teaches: Fear is shown as a new cause of karma before the fruit comes, which extends the quatrain's advice on taking fruit that has arrived.

gains.a: the quatrain's picture of fruit taken calmly as old desert, which the brother states only as the uselessness of fear
gains.b: a case of the advice under the nearest threat, two captives of a sacrifice, where calm is hardest to keep

links.note: The brother recalls births among animals driven by old deeds; the Siddhar asks when he will say enough to births as stone, tree, fish, bird and grass.
links.teaches: The recalled animal births become the very cry of 'enough' that the pair will act on, so the epic gives the Siddhar's wish a remembered cause.

gains.a: the first-person plea to end the lower births, which in the epic is only recounted as past
gains.b: a stated cause of those lower births, old deeds that drive the soul among beasts, with the siblings' own kin as the killers

links.note: The epic says deeds whirl the soul like a wheel through the four states; the couplet names craving as the seed of unceasing birth.
links.teaches: The epic gives the wheel's driver as deeds and the Kural gives craving, so the two books hold different roots of the same round of birth.

gains.a: a named seed of the wheel in craving, which the verse leaves unsaid
gains.b: a picture of the wheel itself, four states and births past counting, which the couplet states only as 'birth'

links.note: The epic says even Indra-like lords of the gods lost their forms; the quatrain says kings on elephants under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and no one is left over.
links.teaches: The quatrain's visible proof that kings die is stretched by the epic to the gods, so no rank in any world offers refuge from loss.

gains.a: a human instance to rest the claim on, kings borne off whom a reader has seen, where it offers gods only by doctrine
gains.b: a reach beyond the visible, to ranks above the world of men, so heaven too is no way out

links.note: The epic likens death and birth to putting off a cloth and leaving a house for another; the couplet likens death to sleep and birth to waking.
links.teaches: The epic's cloth and house are things a person does and leaves, while the Kural's sleep is something that happens to one, so the two images differ on whether the change is in the soul's hands.

gains.a: a figure of death as a daily act with no break in the one who lives on, to calm a frightened girl
gains.b: a purpose beyond mere statement, a comfort spoken at the moment of arrest, where the couplet only describes

links.note: The brother's thought is that women's minds lack firmness; the Kural names firmness, called karpu, as the greatest thing in a woman.
links.teaches: Both books turn on a woman's firmness, but the epic locates it in renunciation and the Kural in chastity, so firmness is not the same virtue in the two.

gains.a: a firmness of mind that is not wifely, here set on leaving life, which the Kural's word does not reach
gains.b: a rival test of the same word, a woman who stands firm in leaving the world and not in keeping her husband

links.note: The brother bids his sister think of the soul as other than the body and leave it in the victors' refuge; the couplet likens the tie of body and life to a bird flying off from its nest.
links.teaches: The couplet calls the tie light and the epic makes it a choice to be carried out, so the same lightness is turned into an act of leaving.

gains.a: the idea that the tie to the body is a loose one, which makes its giving up no loss
gains.b: a pair who act on the image, two who choose the departure and say where they go

links.note: The poet says the soul is stainless and other than the body and that its karma is not its own nature; Tirumular says the stains go only when the sun of grace stands over them.
links.teaches: The epic leaves the stain's end to the soul's own knowledge of itself, while Tirumular needs a light from outside, so the two give opposite sources for the freeing.

gains.a: a rival account in which the stain leaves only when an outside light appears, which shows how much the epic leaves to the soul's own knowing
gains.b: a case of a stainless soul known apart from the body with no god's presence in the account

source_issues: 34 line 1 reads மன்னை, perhaps for அன்னை.
28 line 2 and 50 line 3 are damaged or unclear.
37, 38 and 39 give measures of bodies in the Jain cosmology that are obscure in lines 3-4.
